I want you to establish lasting connections with the right people, and for that reason it would be wise to keep unsuitable acquaintances to a minimum. So, if you are still living in this area when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your closeness to his sisters won’t draw you into a friendship with his wife. She will probably be nothing more than some uneducated farmer’s daughter.”

“Of course. Yes. Though I don’t think Mr. Martin would marry anyone who hadn’t received some education—and been brought up very well. Still, I don’t mean to put my judgment above yours, and I’m sure I won’t want to become acquainted with his wife. I shall always be very fond of the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and I should be terribly sorry to lose them, because they are just as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, I certainly ought to avoid visiting her if I can.”

Emma watched Harriet through the changing opinions of this speech and detected no alarming signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma hoped that his influence went no further, and that Harriet would present no serious obstacle to any friendly arrangement Emma might make herself.

The very next day they encountered Mr. Martin while walking along the Donwell road. He was walking too. After giving Emma a deeply respectful look, he turned to her companion with unmistakable pleasure. Emma welcomed this chance to inspect him. Walking a few yards ahead while they talked, she soon observed enough with her sharp eyes to form an opinion of Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was very tidy, and he looked like a sensible young man, but there was nothing else to recommend his looks. She thought that, once Harriet compared him with gentlemen, he would surely lose whatever place he had gained in her affections. Harriet did appreciate good manners; without prompting, she had remarked on Emma’s father’s gentleness with admiration as well as surprise. Mr. Martin looked as though he had no conception of manners.

They talked for only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting. Harriet then ran up to her, smiling and so excited that Miss Woodhouse hoped to calm her down very soon.

“Just imagine our meeting him like that! How strange! He said it was pure chance that he hadn’t gone around by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever walked along this road. He thought we went toward Randalls most days.”

He was short but stood remarkably straight, and his voice was the most pleasing I had ever heard. He opened his lecture by reviewing the history of chemistry and the advances made by its various scholars, speaking the names of the greatest discoverers with passionate admiration. Then he briefly surveyed the science as it now stood and explained many of its basic terms. After demonstrating a few introductory experiments, he ended with a tribute to modern chemistry whose words I will never forget:

“The early teachers of this science,” he said, “promised impossible things and accomplished nothing. Today’s masters make few promises. They know that metals cannot be transformed into other metals and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem fit only for grubbing in dirt, whose eyes seem meant only to peer into microscopes or crucibles, have truly worked miracles. They enter nature’s deepest recesses and reveal what she does in her secret places. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered the circulation of the blood and the properties of the air we breathe. They have gained new powers that are almost limitless. They can command the thunder of heaven, imitate an earthquake, and even confront the invisible world with likenesses of its own shadows.”

These were the professor’s words—or, I should say, the words of fate itself, spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt my soul wrestling with a tangible enemy. One after another, the keys controlling my entire being were struck; chord followed chord, until a single thought, a single idea, a single purpose filled my mind. So much has already been accomplished, cried Frankenstein’s soul; I will accomplish more, far more. Following the path others have marked, I will open a new route, investigate unknown powers, and reveal to the world creation’s deepest mysteries.

I did not close my eyes that night. Everything within me was in revolt and confusion. I sensed that order would eventually emerge, but I could do nothing to bring it about. Gradually, after dawn, I fell asleep. When I woke, the previous night’s thoughts seemed like a dream. All that remained was my determination to resume my former studies and dedicate myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private he was even gentler and more engaging than in public. The dignity that had marked his bearing during the lecture gave way, in his own home, to the warmest friendliness and kindness.

“Some time passed before I recovered enough to take care of the balloon’s usual needs. When I finally inspected it closely, I was greatly relieved to find it undamaged. All my equipment was safe, and luckily I had lost neither ballast nor food. In fact, I had fastened everything so securely that there was no chance of losing it. My watch showed six o’clock. I was still rising quickly, and the barometer put my height at three and three-quarter miles. Directly below me on the ocean was a small black object, a little longer than it was wide. It seemed about the size of a child’s domino and looked very much like one. Through my telescope I could clearly see that it was a British ship carrying ninety-four guns. It was sailing as close to the wind as possible, pitching heavily in the waves, with its bow pointing west-southwest. Apart from that ship, I saw only sea, sky, and the sun, which had risen long before.

“It is time I explained to Your Excellencies the purpose of this dangerous journey. You will remember that my desperate circumstances in Rotterdam had finally led me to decide to kill myself. I did not actually hate life itself. Rather, the miseries brought on by my situation had tormented me beyond what I could bear. I wanted to live, yet I was tired of living. In that state of mind, the treatise I found on the bookseller’s stall suggested a possible escape. At last I made my decision. I would depart but remain alive; I would leave the world but still exist. To stop speaking in riddles, I resolved to face whatever happened and try to make my way to the moon. Now, so that you will not think me madder than I really am, I shall explain as well as I can the reasoning behind my belief. Difficult and unquestionably dangerous as such a journey would be, I thought it was not wholly beyond what a bold person could accomplish.

“The first question was the moon’s actual distance from the earth. The average distance between the centers of the two planets is 59.9643 times the earth’s radius at the equator, or only about 237,000 miles. I say average distance because we must remember that the moon travels in an ellipse. The eccentricity of that ellipse amounts to no less than 0.05484 of its major semi-axis—that is, half its longest diameter—and the earth’s center lies at one of its focal points. If I could somehow arrange to meet the moon at perigee, when it is nearest the earth, the distance I have just given would be considerably reduced.”
